title: How Taxidermy Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore taxidermy: its origins in leather tanning and specimen preservation by naturalists like James Cook and Darwin, the crude early stuffing methods, and the 1970s shift to polyurethane foam molds. They cover costs (bear rug about $1,000, standing bear about $2,000, deer shoulder mount $500-$700, fish about $18 per inch, bird around $200-$400), the step-by-step process for fish, deer, and birds (skinning, salting with borax, carving molds, glass eyes), taxidermy schools, rogue or carcass taxidermy, the Jackalope legend from Wyoming, and tips for handling road kill. The episode closes with a listener email from Julia about a sorority thief and kleptomania.

segments.title: Intro and taxidermy in movies
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about taxidermy in film, mentioning Norman Bates's office in Psycho, and a listener request inspired by a Bass Pro Shop visit. Chuck shares a story about a hawk killed by a broken window and the Georgia law protecting hawks.

segments.title: History of taxidermy
segments.summary: Taxidermy began in England out of need for usable leather from tanning hides, and naturalists such as James Cook and Darwin used it to preserve specimens. Early methods gutted animals and stuffed them with straw, which failed as eyes, noses and teeth rotted. Plastic and rubber substitute tongues were developed later.

segments.title: Great Taxidermy Revolution and the profession
segments.summary: Until the 1970s taxidermy stuffing stayed largely the same, then the Great Taxidermy Revolution replaced stuffing with polyurethane foam molds. Taxidermists are described as artists, sculptors and craftsmen, and the work ranges from hobbyists to museum-level specialists.

segments.title: Costs and turnaround time
segments.summary: A bear skin rug costs about a thousand dollars and a standing bear about two thousand. A deer shoulder and antler mount runs about five to six hundred dollars. Fish cost about eighteen dollars per inch. Turnaround is slow because there are few taxidermists and skins are sent out for commercial tanning.

segments.title: Fish mounting process
segments.summary: Fish lose color as they dry, so they must be painted scale by scale. Saltwater fish are often replicated from photos in synthetic materials. For skin mounts, the meat and bones are removed, borax and salt are injected, the skin is salted to prevent shrinking, and glass eyes are inserted. Sawdust may be used for flat plaques, while curved poses use foam molds.

segments.title: Deer taxidermy process
segments.summary: Deer taxidermy starts with skinning the deer into a cape with as few cuts as possible. Accurate measurements are taken to build a foam mold, the skull is discarded and antlers kept, and salt preserves the skin and hair follicles. The skin is then slipped over the mold, sewn up, and mounted on a plaque with glass eyes inserted.

segments.title: Bird taxidermy, schools, and road kill tips
segments.summary: Birds are washed, dried with a hair dryer, salted, and given clay heads and foam bodies, with wires under the wings tied with dental floss. Taxidermy schools cost two to four thousand dollars. The hosts advise checking a taxidermist's work and handling road kill carefully, such as storing a hawk in pantyhose and wrapping fish in a wet towel.

segments.title: Jackalope and rogue taxidermy
segments.summary: The jackalope is a shoulder-mounted rabbit with antlers, said to have been created in the 1930s by the Mayor Rick brothers, amateur taxidermists in Wyoming, though the story may be legend. Rogue taxidermy, also called carcass art, is discussed through the Crappy Taxidermy website. The hosts also advise not calling taxidermists to nag about pickup times.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with a sign-off and website plug.
